title: Part 2, Chapter 57
paragraphs: Which tells how Don Quixote took his leave of the duke, and what passed between him and the witty, brazen Altisidora, one of the duchess’s maids

Don Quixote now decided it was time to give up the idle life he was leading in the castle. He imagined that his absence was being sorely felt elsewhere while he let himself stay shut away and inactive among the endless comforts and pleasures his hosts heaped on him as a knight, and he believed, too, that he would one day have to give heaven a strict accounting for all that laziness and seclusion. So one day he asked the duke and duchess for permission to depart. They granted it, while making it plain that they were genuinely sorry to see him go.

The duchess handed Sancho Panza the letters from his wife, and he wept over them, saying, “Who would have guessed that all the grand hopes the news of my governorship stirred up in the breast of my wife Teresa Panza would come down to this — me heading back to the wandering adventures of my master Don Quixote of La Mancha? Still, I’m pleased my Teresa did the proper thing in sending the acorns; if she hadn’t sent them I’d have been hurt, and she’d have looked ungrateful. One comfort is that nobody can call that present a bribe, since I already had the government when she sent it, and it’s only fair that people who’ve had a kindness done them should show some thanks, even if it’s with a small thing. The plain truth is, I went into the government naked and I come out of it naked, so I can say with a clear conscience — and that’s no small thing — ‘naked I was born, naked I find myself; I neither lose nor gain.’”

So Sancho talked to himself on the day of their departure, while Don Quixote, who had said his farewells to the duke and duchess the night before, came out early in the morning in full armor into the castle courtyard. The whole household was watching him from the galleries, and the duke and duchess came out to see him off as well. Sancho sat on his Dapple with his saddlebags, his valise, and his provisions, perfectly delighted, because the duke’s majordomo — the same man who had played the part of the Trifaldi — had slipped him a little purse containing two hundred gold crowns to cover the expenses of the road, though Don Quixote as yet knew nothing about it. While everyone, as has been said, stood watching him, the brazen and witty Altisidora suddenly raised her voice from among the duennas and waiting-maids and cried out in mournful tones:

Listen, cruel knight;
pull up your reins — what need is there
to drive your spurs into the flanks
of that badly broken steed?
What is it you are fleeing?
I am no dragon in your way,
not even a sheep,
but a tender young lamb gone astray.
You have jilted a maiden
as lovely to behold
as any nymph of Diana
or the Venus of old.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

In your claws, pitiless robber,
you carry off as your prey
the heart of a meek
and loving maid today.
Three kerchiefs you have stolen,
and of garters a pair,
from legs that outshine
the whitest marble anywhere;
and the sighs that pursue you
would burn down to the ground
two thousand cities of Troy,
if that many could be found.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

May no drop of mercy
ever be granted to Sancho,
and may your Dulcinea
remain enchanted still;
may your treachery to me
find its punishment in her,
for in my country the righteous
often pay for the sinner.
May your grandest adventures
end in defeat and shame,
may your joys be nothing but dreams,
and your love forgotten like your name.
Bireno, Æneas — what worse name can I call you?
May Barabbas go with you! May every evil befall you!

All the time the unhappy Altisidora was lamenting in this fashion, Don Quixote stood staring at her; then, without a word of reply to her, he turned to Sancho and said, “Sancho, my friend, I implore you by the lives of your ancestors to tell me the truth: have you, by any chance, taken the three kerchiefs and the garters this lovesick maiden is talking about?”
To this Sancho answered, “The three kerchiefs I do have; but as for the garters — they’re as far away as ‘over the hills of Úbeda.’”

The duchess was astonished at Altisidora’s nerve. She knew the girl was bold, lively, and impudent, but not, she thought, to the point of daring a liberty like this; and since no one had warned her of the joke, her amazement was all the greater. The duke, wanting to keep the game going, said, “It strikes me as poorly done, sir knight, that after the hospitality you have enjoyed in this very castle you should have presumed to make off with three kerchiefs at the least, to say nothing of my maid’s garters. It argues a bad heart and sits ill with your reputation. Give back her garters, or else I challenge you to mortal combat — and I am not afraid of any rascally enchanters changing or swapping my face the way they changed the face of the man who fought you into that of my lackey, Tosilos.”

“God forbid,” said Don Quixote, “that I should ever draw my sword against your illustrious person, from whom I have received so many favors. The kerchiefs I will return, since Sancho says he has them; but the garters are out of the question, for I do not have them and neither does he — and if this maid of yours will search her hiding-places, I promise you she will find them there. I have never been a thief, my lord duke, and I never mean to be one as long as I live, provided God does not withdraw his keeping from me. This damsel, by her own admission, speaks as a woman in love, and for that I bear no blame; so I have no pardon to ask, either of her or of your excellence, whom I beg to think better of me, and once again to give me leave to continue my journey.”

“And may God speed it so well, Señor Don Quixote,” said the duchess, “that we may always hear good news of your deeds. Go, and God be with you; for the longer you linger here, the hotter you make the fires in the hearts of the damsels who look at you — and as for this one of mine, I will discipline her so thoroughly that from now on she will not misbehave with her eyes or her tongue.”

“One word more, O valiant Don Quixote, and only one — hear me out,” said Altisidora. “I beg your pardon about the theft of the garters; for by God and on my soul, I am wearing them this minute, and I have made the same blunder as the man who went off hunting for his donkey while he was sitting on its back.”
“What did I tell you?” said Sancho. “A fine one I am to go hiding stolen goods! If I’d wanted any part of that trade, I had chances enough handed to me in my government.”

Don Quixote bowed his head and saluted the duke and duchess and all the onlookers; then, wheeling Rocinante around, with Sancho following on Dapple, he rode out of the castle and set his course for Saragossa.
